question: How are documents turned into the vocabulary of index terms (tokenization, normalization, stemming) and how are postings lists extended (skip pointers, biword and positional indexes) to run faster and answer phrase and proximity queries?
contributions: Defines the document unit, token, type and term, and the tokenization problems per language (Section 2.1-2.2.1)
Covers stop words, normalization and equivalence classing, stemming and lemmatization (Sections 2.2.2-2.2.4)
Skip pointers for faster postings intersection (Section 2.3)
Biword, positional and combination indexes for phrase and proximity queries (Section 2.4)

results.claim: Over time IR systems moved from large stop lists to tiny ones to none, and web search engines generally use none.
results.setup: General trend in IR systems, no named collection; Fig 2.5 shows a 25-word list from Reuters-RCV1.
results.quote: quite large stop lists (200–300 terms) to very small stop lists (7–12 terms)

results.claim: Rule of thumb: a positional index is 2 to 4 times as large as a non-positional index.
results.setup: Rough rule of thumb, depends on document type and language; specific numbers deferred to Tables 5.1 and 5.6.
results.quote: some rough rules of thumb are to expect a positional index to be 2 to 4 times as large as a non-positional index

results.claim: A compressed positional index is about one third to one half the size of the raw text.
results.setup: Rule of thumb, after removal of markup, relative to the original uncompressed documents.
results.quote: a compressed positional index to be about one third to one half the size of the raw text

results.claim: Positional postings grow with document length: a term with frequency 1 in 1000 terms needs 1 entry per posting in a 1000-term document and 100 in a 100,000-term document.
results.setup: Term with frequency 1 in 1000 terms on average; document sizes 1000 and 100,000 terms; average web page under 1000 terms, SEC filings and books reach 100,000.
results.quote: large documents cause an increase of two orders of magnitude in the space required to store the postings list
results.note: The table in the text gives 1, 1 for the 1000-term row and 1, 100 for the 100,000-term row.

results.claim: A positional index changes Boolean query complexity from the number of documents to the number of tokens in the collection.
results.setup: Intersection over positional postings; T is total tokens, N is number of documents.
results.quote: the complexity of a Boolean query is Θ(T) rather than Θ(N)

results.claim: Postings intersection without skip pointers takes O(m + n) for list lengths m and n.
results.setup: Basic two-list merge from Section 1.3, linear in total postings entries.
results.quote: the intersection takes O(m + n) operations

results.claim: Heuristic for skip placement: sqrt(P) evenly spaced skip pointers for a postings list of length P.
results.setup: Postings list of length P; stated to work well in practice but ignores the distribution of query terms; skips help only AND queries, only on original (not intermediate) lists.
results.quote: for a postings list of length P, use
results.note: The square root sign is printed on a separate line in the text extraction, so the quote stops before it.

results.claim: Moffat and Zobel (1996) report conjunctive queries about five times faster with skip pointers.
results.setup: Skip pointers vs none; system and collection not given in the chapter.
results.quote: conjunctive queries running about five times faster with the use of skip pointers
results.note: Contradicted in the same paragraph by Bahle et al. (2002), who find skip lists slow search with modern CPUs because disk I/O dominates; Strohman and Croft (2007) again find gains in an in-memory multicore design.

results.claim: Williams et al. (2004): a combined phrase, positional and next-word index finishes a typical mix of web phrase queries in one quarter of the time of a positional index alone.
results.setup: Mixture of web phrase queries; scheme combines phrase index, positional index and a partial next word index.
results.quote: completed in one quarter of the time taken by use of a positional index alone

results.claim: The same Williams et al. (2004) scheme takes 26% more space than a positional index alone.
results.setup: Same scheme and web phrase query mix as the one-quarter-time result.
results.quote: while taking up 26% more space than use of a positional index alone

results.claim: Adding The Who as a phrase index entry speeds that query by a factor of 1000, but Britney Spears only by about 3.
results.setup: Illustrative: speedup is largest when the words are individually common but the phrase is rare; no collection named.
results.quote: may speed up that query by a factor of 1000
results.note: Britney Spears figure: 'a speedup factor to that query of about 3'.

results.claim: As many as 10% of web queries are phrase queries, and many more are implicit phrase queries.
results.metric: share of web queries that are phrase queries
results.setup: Stated without citation in Section 2.4.
results.quote: As many as 10% of web queries are phrase queries
results.note: Section 2.5 cites Johnson et al. (2006): 11.7% in two 2002 web query logs, and Kammenhuber et al. (2006): 3% in a different data set. So the 10% in the body sits between two reported figures.

results.claim: Johnson et al. (2006) report 11.7% of queries in two 2002 web query logs contained phrase queries.
results.setup: Two 2002 web query logs.
results.quote: Johnson et al. (2006) report that 11.7% of all queries in two 2002 web query logs contained phrase queries
results.note: Kammenhuber et al. (2006) report only 3% for a different data set.

results.claim: Hollink et al. (2004): diacritic removal gains up to 23% MAP over a baseline across 8 European languages.
results.metric: percent change in mean average precision
results.unit: % change in MAP over baseline system
results.setup: 8 European languages; especially helpful for Finnish, French and Swedish.
results.quote: diacritic removal gains up to 23%

results.claim: Hollink et al. (2004): stemming improved MAP 30% for Finnish and 10% for Spanish, but only 0-5% for most languages including English; a lemmatizer was poorer still.
results.metric: percent change in mean average precision from stemming
results.setup: 8 European languages, language-specific methods vs baseline system.
results.quote: Stemming helped markedly for Finnish (30% improvement) and Spanish (10% improvement)
results.note: Range for other languages: 'the gain from stemming was in the range 0–5%'; the en dash is a Unicode character.

results.claim: Hollink et al. (2004): compound splitting gained 25% for Swedish, 15% for German, 4% for Dutch.
results.metric: percent change in MAP from compound splitting
results.setup: Same study of 8 European languages.
results.quote: Compound splitting gained 25% for Swedish and 15% for German, but only 4% for Dutch

results.claim: Hollink et al. (2004): within-word character 4-grams beat words by 37% (Finnish), 27% (Swedish), 20% (German) and were slightly positive for Dutch, Spanish, English.
results.metric: percent change in MAP from character 4-grams vs words
results.setup: Within-word character 4-gram indexing replacing word indexing; same 8-language study. Tomlinson (2003) is said to present broadly similar results.
results.quote: using within-word character 4-grams rather than words gave gains of 37% in Finnish, 27% in Swedish, and 20% in German

results.claim: Stemming increases recall while harming precision, and for English the aggregate effect of stemming or lemmatization is small because it helps some queries a lot and hurts others a lot.
results.setup: English retrieval; Porter stemmer maps operate, operating, operates, operation, operative, operatives, operational to oper, hurting queries such as operating AND system.
results.quote: Stemming increases recall while harming precision.
results.note: More morphologically rich languages (Spanish, German, Finnish) gain 'quite large gains' per CLEF results, p. 34.

results.claim: Word counts in the tokenization example: 'to sleep perchance to dream' has 5 tokens, 4 types, and 3 terms if 'to' is a stop word.
results.setup: Single sentence to sleep perchance to dream.
results.quote: then there are 5 tokens, but only 4 types

results.claim: About 60% of web pages were in English (Gerrand 2007), and only about one third of blog posts (Sifry 2007).
results.metric: share of web pages in English
results.setup: Web as of 2007 citations.
results.quote: approximately 60% of web pages are in English (Gerrand 2007)

results.claim: Part-of-speech taggers reach about 96% per-tag accuracy.
results.setup: Taggers trained on hand-tagged text; cited via Manning and Schütze (1999, ch. 10); used for extended biwords of the form NX*N.
results.quote: (c. 96% per-tag accuracy)

limits: Published 2008 (online edition April 2009 draft): all of it concerns lexical, Boolean and term-based indexing. There is nothing on dense vectors, learned tokenizers (BPE, WordPiece), neural retrieval or hybrid scoring.

Almost no measurements of its own: quantitative claims are rules of thumb or citations (Hollink 2004, Williams 2004, Moffat and Zobel 1996). The chapter gives no collection, hardware or query-set detail for them.
Stop-word advice is dated: the chapter says web engines use none, and the Section 2.2.2 argument rests on postings compression (Section 5.3) and impact-ordered indexes (Section 7.1.5).
Skip-pointer value depends on hardware: the text concedes the optimal encoding changes with CPU, disk and memory speeds, and cites Bahle et al. (2002) against skip lists on disk-bound systems.

Stemming and case-folding advice is for English; the authors say the best amount of equivalence classing is 'a fairly open question' and fine details may have little aggregate effect if query and documents are processed consistently.
Footnote 5 says the C.A.T. example was true on Google in Aug. 2005, so that observation is dated.
Exercises 2.1-2.14 have no answers in this PDF.
Figures with Arabic, Chinese and Japanese text did not extract; only captions are available.
practices: Tokenize queries with the same tokenizer as documents, so a character sequence in a text always matches the same sequence typed in a query (p. 24).

Choose the indexing unit by understanding the collection, users and usage; index book chapters or paragraphs rather than whole books because large units give spurious matches and small units miss terms spread across units (pp. 21-22).
Index monetary amounts, numbers and URLs rather than dropping them when users may search for them, such as bug line numbers (p. 24).
Detect the language of a document before choosing language-specific tokenization and normalization, using classifiers on short character subsequences (p. 24).
For German, use a compound splitter; for Chinese and Japanese, either segment words or index character k-grams or bigrams (pp. 25-26, 45).
Prefer no stop list for modern systems, since phrase queries such as President of the United States and titles like To be or not to be are damaged by stopping (p. 27).
Case-fold by lowercasing everything as the practical default, unless users type proper case, in which case truecasing or heuristic lowercasing is an alternative (p. 30).
For accent normalization, ask how users write queries: when they often omit diacritics, equate words to a form without them (p. 29).
Keep expansion lists (asymmetric expansion) rather than equivalence classes when you want, for example, query windows to match Windows but not the reverse (p. 29, Fig 2.6).
Use a stemmer or lemmatizer cautiously for English, with consistent processing of query and document; expect larger gains in Spanish, German and Finnish (pp. 33-34).
Place sqrt(P) evenly spaced skip pointers on a postings list of length P and use them only for AND queries over original lists (p. 37).
Use a positional index as the standard solution for phrase and proximity queries; start intersecting from the least frequent term (p. 41).
Combine a positional index with a phrase or biword index for common phrases, choosing entries where the words are common but the phrase is rare (pp. 43-44).
Use Westlaw/Lexis-Nexis style generalization: for a hyphenated query term search the hyphenated, one-word and two-word forms (p. 25).

terms.definition: an instance of a sequence of characters in some particular document that are grouped together as a useful semantic unit for processing
the class of all tokens containing the same character sequence
a (perhaps normalized) type that is included in the IR system's dictionary
the task of chopping a character sequence up into pieces, called tokens, perhaps at the same time throwing away certain characters, such as punctuation
extremely common words of little value in selecting documents, excluded from the vocabulary entirely; a stop list is usually the most frequent terms by collection frequency, hand-filtered
the total number of times each term appears in the document collection
the process of canonicalizing tokens so that matches occur despite superficial differences in the character sequences of the tokens
sets of tokens mapped to one term, normally named after one member of the set
reducing all letters to lower case
making the decision of when to case-fold with a machine learning sequence model that uses more features
a crude heuristic process that chops off the ends of words in the hope of reducing inflectional (and often derivational) forms to a common base form
doing reduction properly with a vocabulary and morphological analysis of words, normally removing inflectional endings only and returning the lemma
a postings list augmented at indexing time with skip pointers, shortcuts that avoid processing parts of the list that will not figure in the results
an index that treats every pair of consecutive terms in a document as a phrase and makes each biword a vocabulary term
an index that includes variable length word sequences
an index storing for each term postings of the form docID: <position1, position2, ...>, where each position is a token index in the document
for each term, a record of the terms that follow it in a document
the choice of unit (book, chapter, paragraph, sentence) at which text is indexed as a document

code.snippet: INTERSECTWITHSKIPS(p1, p2): answer <- <>; while p1 != NIL and p2 != NIL do if docID(p1) = docID(p2) then ADD(answer, docID(p1)); p1 <- next(p1); p2 <- next(p2) else if docID(p1) < docID(p2) then if hasSkip(p1) and (docID(skip(p1)) <= docID(p2)) then while hasSkip(p1) and (docID(skip(p1)) <= docID(p2)) do p1 <- skip(p1) else p1 <- next(p1) else (symmetric for p2); return answer

POSITIONALINTERSECT(p1, p2, k): for documents with docID(p1) = docID(p2), scan positions pp1, pp2; if |pos(pp1) - pos(pp2)| <= k then ADD(l, pos(pp2)) else if pos(pp2) > pos(pp1) then break; drop l[0] while |l[0] - pos(pp1)| > k; ADD(answer, <docID, pos(pp1), ps>) for each ps in l
SSES -> SS (caresses -> caress); IES -> I (ponies -> poni); SS -> SS (caress -> caress); S -> (cats -> cat)
